summary.text: A thunderstorm, also called an electrical or lightning storm, is a storm marked by lightning and thunder that forms in cumulonimbus clouds.
It grows when warm, moist air rises fast, cools and condenses, releasing heat that keeps the air rising; it needs moisture, unstable air and a lifting force.
Thunderstorms can bring damaging downburst winds, large hail, flash floods and even tornadoes, and every one passes through developing, mature and dissipating stages.

facts.label: Seen beyond Earth
facts.value: On Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and probably Venus

items.prompt: A thunderstorm drops no rain at all, yet a forest fire breaks out under it. What most likely started the fire?

options.label: Hot downdraft winds drying the trees

items.explain: Dry thunderstorms can spark wildfires from the heat of the cloud-to-ground lightning that comes with them.

items.prompt: Just before a thunderstorm reaches you, a sudden cold gust sweeps across the ground. Where does that cold wind come from?

options.label: Falling rain dragging cold air down to spread out
Warm air being sucked up into the cloud
Lightning heating the air around it
The ground cooling once the sun is blocked

items.explain: Falling droplets create a downdraft that pulls cold air down, and it spreads out at the surface, sometimes as strong winds.

items.prompt: Rising air in a growing storm cloud cools, but it keeps climbing past cooler air around it. What keeps it going?
items.explain: Condensing moisture releases latent heat, so the rising air cools less than its surroundings and keeps ascending.

items.prompt: A storm-chasing guide wants the best odds of seeing the strongest, most severe kind of thunderstorm. Which should they hunt for?
items.explain: Of the three types, supercell thunderstorms are the strongest and most severe, and they rotate like cyclones.

items.prompt: A warm, humid day has plenty of unstable air, yet no storms form until a cold front arrives. What was missing before?

options.label: A force to lift the air

items.explain: Thunderstorms need moisture, an unstable air mass and a lifting force; a front can supply the push upward.

items.prompt: In its mature stage, a storm's rising air stops climbing at a certain height. Why does it stop?

options.label: It runs into warmer air it cannot rise through
It runs out of water vapour to condense
It freezes solid and falls as hail
It reaches the edge of space

items.explain: The warmed air keeps rising until it meets an area of warmer air, often the tropopause, and can rise no farther.

paragraphs.heading: Lightning and thunder
paragraphs.text: A thunderstorm is a storm that brings lightning and thunder, and it also goes by the names electrical storm and lightning storm. It grows inside a cumulonimbus cloud. Weaker ones are sometimes called thundershowers. Most come with strong winds and often heavy rain, and some bring snow, sleet or hail, though a few drop little or no rain at all.

paragraphs.heading: Three ingredients
paragraphs.text: A thunderstorm needs moisture, unstable air and something that lifts the air. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises while the cooler air settles below. Thunderstorms come from warm, moist air rising fast, and that rise needs a push from a front, a shortwave trough or some other system. As the moist air climbs it cools, and part of its water vapour condenses into cloud.

paragraphs.heading: The engine inside
paragraphs.text: Condensation gives off energy called latent heat of condensation. That heat keeps the rising air from cooling as much as the air around it, so it carries on climbing. If the atmosphere is unstable enough, this goes on until a cumulonimbus cloud forms, which can tower more than 20 kilometres (12 mi) high and produce lightning and thunder. To judge how tall clouds may grow, forecasters lean on indices like the lifted index and convective available potential energy (CAPE).

paragraphs.heading: A storm's life
paragraphs.text: Every thunderstorm passes through three stages: developing, mature and dissipating. An average storm is about 24 km (15 mi) across, and each stage lasts around 30 minutes on average. In the first, or cumulus, stage, moisture is carried upward, lifted by sun-warmed ground sending up thermals, by two winds meeting, or by wind pushed up rising land. The heat released as vapour condenses keeps the air rising in an updraft, and a low-pressure zone forms in and under the young storm. In the mature stage the warm air rises until it meets warmer air and can go no higher, often at the tropopause.

paragraphs.heading: Rain and wind
paragraphs.text: Once the rising air reaches its dew point, vapour turns into water drops or ice. The drops fall a long way through the cloud, bumping into others and growing as they go. Falling drops drag cold air down with them in a downdraft, and that cold air spreads out at ground level, sometimes as the strong winds people link with thunderstorms. Storms can form anywhere but are most common in the mid-latitudes, where warm, moist tropical air runs into cooler polar air.

paragraphs.heading: When storms turn dangerous
paragraphs.text: There are three types: single-cell, multi-cell and supercell. Supercells are the strongest, and some of the most persistent severe storms are supercells that rotate the way cyclones do. Most damage comes from downburst winds, large hail and flash floods from heavy rain, and stronger cells can spin up tornadoes and waterspouts. Even a dry storm with no rain can do harm, since the heat of its cloud-to-ground lightning can set off wildfires. In the tropics and subtropics, large storm systems shaped by favourable wind shear can lead to hurricanes.

paragraphs.heading: Watching storms here and beyond
paragraphs.text: People study thunderstorms with weather radar, weather stations and video. They are not only found on Earth: thunderstorms have been seen on Jupiter, Saturn and Neptune, and probably on Venus too.
